title: Fuel-Vapor Management — 3.7L Duratec
introduction: The 3.7L Duratec evaporative emissions system gives fuel vapor a holding place and a later destination in the engine. I think of the canister as a waiting room, with separate valves managing the engine-bound and outside-air routes. This overview explains the component roles; it does not establish hose locations, valve test conditions or a repair procedure.

edits.text: The evaporative emissions (EVAP) system prevents fuel-vapor hydrocarbons from escaping into the atmosphere. It stores the vapors, then routes them to the engine to be consumed during normal engine operation.
edits.why: Capture and consumption happen as parts of the same process. This vapor-handling job differs from delivering liquid fuel to the engine.

edits.text: The EVAP system includes these components, each with a distinct role:
edits.why: I keep the component names separate when reading further information: a canister, purge valve and vent solenoid are different parts.

edits.text: EVAP canister: activated carbon captures and stores fuel vapor until it is drawn into the engine during purging.
edits.why: Removing the stored vapor during purge leaves the carbon ready to capture more.

edits.text: EVAP canister purge valve: an electrically controlled valve that regulates vapor flow from the canister toward the engine intake.
edits.why: “Purge” identifies the engine-bound route, which empties stored vapor from the canister for combustion.

edits.text: EVAP canister vent solenoid: an electrically operated valve that controls the canister’s connection to outside air.
edits.why: The vent manages the outside-air route. Its similar name does not make it interchangeable with the purge valve.

edits.text: Fuel Tank Pressure (FTP) sensor and tube: the components associated with sensing pressure in the fuel tank.
Easy Fuel (capless) fuel tank filler pipe: the capless refueling entry included in this system.
